translations.text: Now, the teaching of yoga.

notes: Vyāsa: atha marks the beginning of the subject: the treatise that teaches yoga is to be understood as begun. Yoga is meditative absorption (samādhi), and that is a property of the mind in all its states. The states of the mind are five: restless, dull, distracted, one-pointed and ceased. Absorption in a distracted mind, being subordinate to distraction, does not count as yoga. That which, in a one-pointed mind, lights up a thing as it really is, wears away the afflictions, loosens the bonds of action and turns the mind towards cessation is called yoga with cognition (saṃprajñāta); when all activities have ceased, the absorption is beyond cognition (asaṃprajñāta).

words.meaning: the cessation of the activities of the mind

translations.text: Yoga is the cessation of the activities of the mind.

notes: Vyāsa: since the sūtra does not say ‘all’, yoga with cognition is also called yoga. The mind has the three guṇas, since it tends to illumination, activity and inertia. When, with the last trace of rajas gone, it rests in its own nature and is nothing but the discernment that sattva and the Puruṣa are different, it turns to the meditation called ‘cloud of dharma’. The power of consciousness is unchanging, does not pass into objects, and is pure and endless; this discernment, being of the nature of sattva, is its opposite. So the mind, dispassionate towards that too, brings even that discernment to cessation and stays with latent impressions alone: that is seedless absorption, beyond cognition.

translations.text: Then the seer abides in his own nature.

notes: Vyāsa: then the power of consciousness is established in its own nature, as in soleness. When the mind is turned outwards it is so too, yet does not appear so.
kaivalya, ‘soleness’: the state of the Puruṣa alone (kevala), resting in its own nature, free of the guṇas (4.34).

words.meaning: likeness in form to the activities

translations.text: At other times he has the same form as the activities.

notes: Vyāsa: when the mind is turned outwards, the Puruṣa's activity is not distinct from the activities of the mind. The mind is like a magnet: it serves merely by being near, and as what is seen it belongs to the Puruṣa, its owner. So the cause of the Puruṣa's awareness of the mind's activities is his beginningless connection with it.

translations.text: The activities are of five kinds, afflicted and unafflicted.

notes: Vyāsa: the afflicted are caused by the afflictions and are the field in which the store of action grows. The unafflicted have discernment for their object and oppose the working of the guṇas; they remain unafflicted even when they fall in a stream of the afflicted. Activities produce latent impressions of their own kind, and impressions produce activities: so the wheel of activities and impressions turns without rest.

words.meaning: valid knowledge, error, verbal construction, sleep and memory

translations.text: They are valid knowledge, error, verbal construction, sleep and memory.
The kinds of valid knowledge are perception, inference and testimony.

notes: Vyāsa: perception is the activity of the mind, coloured by an outer thing through the channel of the senses, which chiefly determines the particular in an object that is both general and particular. Inference chiefly determines the general, through a relation present in things of the same class and absent from things of another: the moon and stars move, because they reach another place, like Caitra. Testimony is the hearer's knowledge of a thing from the words of a trustworthy person who has seen or inferred it.

words.meaning: not resting on the form of the thing

translations.text: Error is false knowledge, not resting on the form of the thing.

notes: Vyāsa: it is not valid knowledge because valid knowledge, whose object is the thing as it is, cancels it, as the sight of one moon cancels the sight of two. This is the fivefold ignorance, the afflictions of 2.3, also named darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom and blind gloom.

translations.text: Verbal construction follows from knowledge of words and is empty of any real thing.

notes: Vyāsa: it falls under neither valid knowledge nor error. Though there is no real thing, usage rests on the power of the knowledge of words: as in ‘consciousness is the nature of the Puruṣa’, where, since the Puruṣa is consciousness itself, nothing is predicated of anything; or ‘the Puruṣa is inactive’, ‘the arrow stands still’, where only the absence of a property is understood.

words.meaning: resting on the notion of absence

translations.text: Sleep is the activity that rests on the notion of absence.

notes: Vyāsa: it is a particular cognition, because one reflects on it on waking: ‘I slept well, my mind is clear’; ‘I slept badly, my mind is dull’; ‘I slept in a deep stupor, my limbs are heavy’. That reflection, and the memories based on it, could not be without an experience. So sleep too is to be brought to cessation in absorption, like the other cognitions.

words.meaning: the not letting slip of an object once experienced

translations.text: Memory is the not letting slip of an object once experienced.

notes: Vyāsa: a cognition, coloured by its object and showing the form of both the object and the grasping of it, sets up a latent impression of the same kind, and that impression produces a memory of both. Memory is of two kinds: of what is imagined, in dream, and of what is not imagined, in waking. All these activities are of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion, and all are to be brought to cessation; then absorption follows, with cognition or beyond it.

translations.text: Their cessation comes by practice and dispassion.

notes: Vyāsa: the river of the mind flows both ways, towards good and towards evil. Flowing down the slope of discernment towards soleness it carries good; flowing down the slope of non-discernment towards the cycle of birth and death it carries evil. Dispassion dams the stream towards objects; the practice of discerning sight opens the stream of discernment. So cessation depends on both.

translations.text: Of these, practice is the effort for steadiness.

notes: Vyāsa: steadiness is the calm flow of a mind free of activities. Effort is energy, zeal; practice is carrying out the means with the wish to bring that about.

words.meaning: attended to for a long time, without break and with devotion

translations.text: But that is firmly grounded when attended to for a long time, without break and with devotion.

notes: Vyāsa: carried out with austerity, continence, knowledge and faith, it is done with devotion and becomes firmly grounded: it is not suddenly overpowered by the impressions of the outward-turned mind.

words.meaning: of one without thirst for objects seen or heard of in scripture

translations.text: Dispassion is the consciousness of mastery in one without thirst for objects seen or heard of in scripture.

notes: Vyāsa: objects seen are women, food and drink, lordship; those heard of in scripture are heaven, the bodiless state and the state of being merged in Prakṛti. Even in contact with objects divine or not divine, the mind, seeing their faults by the strength of reflection, neither rejects nor takes them up: that freedom from enjoyment is the consciousness of mastery.

words.meaning: from the discernment of the Puruṣa
freedom from thirst for the guṇas

translations.text: The higher dispassion is freedom from thirst for the guṇas, from the discernment of the Puruṣa.

notes: Vyāsa: one who is dispassionate through seeing the faults of objects seen and heard of, and whose understanding is filled by the practice of seeing the Puruṣa, becomes dispassionate towards the guṇas themselves, manifest and unmanifest. The second dispassion is only the clearness of knowledge. When it arises the yogin thinks: ‘what was to be gained is gained; the afflictions to be destroyed are destroyed; the chain of births is cut’. Dispassion is the highest point of knowledge, and soleness follows it without a gap.

words.meaning: from its being accompanied by the forms of gross thought, subtle thought, joy and the sense of ‘I am’

translations.text: (Meditative absorption is) with cognition when it is accompanied by the forms of gross thought, subtle thought, joy and the sense of ‘I am’.

notes: Vyāsa: vitarka is the mind's gross experience of its object, vicāra the subtle; ānanda is gladness; asmitā is the awareness of oneself as one. The first absorption has all four; the second lacks gross thought; the third lacks subtle thought too; the fourth is the sense of ‘I am’ alone. All of them have an object.

words.meaning: preceded by the practice of the notion of cessation
in which latent impressions alone remain

translations.text: The other, preceded by the practice of the notion of cessation, is that in which latent impressions alone remain.

notes: Vyāsa: this is absorption beyond cognition: the cessation of the mind when all activities have set and only impressions remain. Its means is the higher dispassion; a practice that has an object cannot bring it about, so the notion of cessation, which has no object, is made the support. The mind then, without support, is as if it had ceased to be: this is seedless absorption.

words.meaning: of the bodiless and of those merged in Prakṛti

translations.text: For the bodiless and for those merged in Prakṛti it is caused by birth.

notes: Vyāsa: it is of two kinds, caused by a means and caused by birth; the first belongs to yogins. The bodiless are gods: with a mind that works by its own impressions alone they experience something like soleness, and live out the ripening of those impressions. Those merged in Prakṛti likewise experience something like soleness, until the mind, its task unfinished, returns.

words.meaning: preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, meditative absorption and wisdom

translations.text: For the others it is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, meditative absorption and wisdom.

notes: Vyāsa: this is the one caused by a means, and belongs to yogins. Faith is the clearness of the mind; like a kind mother it protects the yogin. In one who has faith and seeks discernment, energy arises; then mindfulness; with mindfulness the mind, untroubled, becomes absorbed; and in the absorbed mind comes the discernment of wisdom, by which he knows a thing as it is. From the practice of that, and from dispassion, comes absorption beyond cognition.

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: For those of keen ardour it is near.

notes: Vyāsa: yogins are of nine kinds, as their means are mild, middling or intense, and each of these as their ardour is mild, middling or keen. What is near is the gaining of absorption and its fruit.

words.meaning: from its being mild, middling or intense

translations.text: Even among these there is a difference, as it is mild, middling or intense.

notes: Vyāsa: keen ardour is itself mildly, middlingly or intensely keen. For the mildly keen it is near, for the middlingly keen nearer, and for the intensely keen whose means are intense it is nearest.

translations.text: Or from devotion to the Lord.

notes: Vyāsa: praṇidhāna is a particular kind of devotion. Drawn by it, the Lord favours the yogin by his mere thought of him; and by that alone the gaining of absorption and its fruit comes nearest.

words.meaning: by afflictions, actions, their ripening and their latent stores

translations.text: The Lord is a distinct Puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, their ripening and their latent stores.

notes: Vyāsa: the afflictions are ignorance and the rest; actions are good and bad; ripening is their fruit; the stores are the latent tendencies that accord with it. These exist in the mind and are ascribed to the Puruṣa as their experiencer, as victory or defeat among soldiers is ascribed to their master. He who is untouched by such experience is the Lord. Many have reached soleness after cutting the three bonds; but the Lord never had, and never will have, any tie with bondage: he is always free and always the Lord. His lordship has no equal and none higher, for of two equals wishing opposite things at once, one must fail.

translations.text: In him the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed.

notes: Vyāsa: the grasping of things past, future and present, singly or together, beyond the senses, is small in one and greater in another: this is the seed of omniscience. Since it admits of more, it must reach a limit, as size does; he in whom it reaches its limit is the omniscient one. Inference shows only that there is such a one; his name and the like are to be learnt from scripture. He has nothing to gain for himself; his purpose is to favour beings, by teaching knowledge and dharma.

translations.text: He is the teacher even of the earlier ones, because he is not limited by time.

notes: Vyāsa: the earlier teachers are limited by time; he whom time does not reach as a limit is their teacher too. As he is there at the beginning of this creation, so he is to be understood at the beginnings of the creations that have passed.

translations.text: The word that denotes him is the syllable Om.

notes: Vyāsa: is the relation of word and thing made by convention, or is it there already, like a lamp and its light? It is there already; the Lord's convention only makes known what exists, as the existing relation of father and son is shown by saying ‘this is his father’. In other creations too the convention is made in the same way.

translations.text: The repetition of it and dwelling on its meaning (are to be practised).

notes: Vyāsa: repetition of Om, and dwelling on the Lord whom it denotes. The mind of the yogin who does both becomes one-pointed. As it is said: ‘From recitation let him pass to yoga, from yoga to recitation; by the perfection of both the supreme Self shines forth.’

words.meaning: the attainment of the inward consciousness

translations.text: From that come the attainment of the inward consciousness and also the absence of obstacles.

notes: Vyāsa: the obstacles, sickness and the rest, do not arise, through devotion to the Lord; and he comes to see his own nature. As the Lord is a Puruṣa, pure, serene, alone, free of trouble, so he knows this Puruṣa, the one who is aware of the understanding.

words.meaning: sickness, dullness, doubt, negligence, laziness, craving, mistaken view, not gaining a stage, and not staying in it

translations.text: Sickness, dullness, doubt, negligence, laziness, craving, mistaken view, not gaining a stage and not staying in it are the distractions of the mind; they are the obstacles.

notes: Vyāsa: sickness is imbalance of the humours, secretions and organs. Dullness is the mind's unfitness for work. Doubt is a thought that touches both sides: ‘it may be so, it may not’. Negligence is not cultivating the means to absorption. Laziness is inactivity from heaviness of body and mind. Craving is the mind's greed for contact with objects. Mistaken view is knowledge by error. The stage is a stage of absorption; not staying is the mind's failure to hold a stage it has gained. These nine arise together with the activities of the mind.

words.meaning: pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, in-breathing and out-breathing

translations.text: Pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, in-breathing and out-breathing go with the distractions.

notes: Vyāsa: pain is of three kinds, from oneself, from other beings and from the gods; it is that which beings, when struck by it, strive to remove. Dejection is the mind's disturbance when a wish is thwarted. In-breathing is the breath drawing in the outer air; out-breathing is its sending out the air within. These belong to the distracted mind, and not to the absorbed mind.

translations.text: To ward them off, the practice of one principle.

notes: Vyāsa: to ward off the distractions one should train the mind to rest on a single principle. He then argues against those for whom the mind is a mere cognition, bound to one object and momentary. On that view every mind is one-pointed and none is distracted; yet the mind is said to become one- pointed when it is withdrawn from everything and settled on one object, so it is not bound to one object at a time. If one-pointedness is taken to be a stream of like cognitions, it cannot be a property of the stream-mind, for, being momentary, there is no one stream-mind; and if it is a property of each cognition in the stream, then every cognition, in a like or an unlike stream, is one-pointed, and a distracted mind is impossible.

Vyāsa: and if cognitions different in nature arose unconnected by one mind, how could one cognition remember what another saw, or experience the fruit of the store of action that another laid up? Whatever answer is contrived for this outdoes the reasoning that cow-dung is milk-rice. It also denies one's own experience: in ‘what I saw I now touch’ the notion ‘I’ stands undivided in the one who has the cognitions, though the cognitions differ. This is grasped by one's own experience; and the force of perception is not overcome by another means of knowledge, which itself works only by the strength of perception. So the mind is one, has many objects, and endures.

words.meaning: of friendliness, compassion, gladness and indifference
towards the happy, the suffering, the virtuous and the wicked

translations.text: The mind is made clear by cultivating friendliness towards the happy, compassion towards the suffering, gladness towards the virtuous and indifference towards the wicked.

notes: Vyāsa: in one who cultivates these, bright dharma arises, and from it the mind becomes clear; clear, it becomes one-pointed and gains steadiness.

words.meaning: by the expulsion and the retention

translations.text: Or by the expulsion and the retention of the breath.

notes: Vyāsa: expulsion is casting out the air of the chest through the nostrils with a particular effort; retention is the control of the breath. By these too one may bring about the steadiness of the mind.

sanskrit.iast: viṣayavatī vā pravṛttir utpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhanī || 35 ||

lines.iast: viṣayavatī vā pravṛttir utpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhanī

padaccheda.iast: viṣayavatī vā pravṛttiḥ utpannā manasaḥ sthiti-nibandhanī
padaccheda.deva: विषयवती वा प्रवृत्तिः उत्पन्ना मनसः स्थिति-निबन्धनी

grammar.en: past passive participle f. nom. sg.

translations.text: Or a direct perception of a sense object, when it has arisen, holds the mind in steadiness.

notes: Vyāsa: for one who fixes the mind on the tip of the nose there is an awareness of divine scent; on the tip of the tongue, of taste; on the palate, of colour; on the middle of the tongue, of touch; on its root, of sound. These hold the mind steady, blow away doubt and become a door to the wisdom of absorption. Though what is learnt from scripture, inference and a teacher is true, so long as no part of it is known by one's own faculties it all seems indirect and gives no firm conviction about subtle things such as liberation. When one part is directly seen, all the rest is believed; and then faith, energy, mindfulness and absorption come without hindrance.

translations.text: Or the sorrowless, luminous (perception).

notes: Vyāsa: ‘a perception, when it has arisen, holds the mind in steadiness’ carries on. For one who fixes the mind in the lotus of the heart there is an awareness of the understanding, whose sattva is shining and like space; it takes the form of the light of sun, moon, planets and gems. Likewise the mind absorbed in the sense of ‘I am’ becomes calm and endless, like a great ocean without waves. These two are the sorrowless perception: the one with an object, and the one that is the sense of ‘I am’ alone.

words.meaning: having for its object one free from passion

translations.text: Or the mind that has for its object one free from passion.

notes: Vyāsa: the yogin's mind, coloured by taking as its support the mind of one free from passion, gains steadiness.

words.meaning: resting on the knowledge had in dream or in sleep

translations.text: Or (the mind) resting on the knowledge had in dream or in sleep.

notes: Vyāsa: the yogin's mind, taking the form of the knowledge of dream or of sleep as its support, gains steadiness.

words.meaning: from meditation on whatever one wishes

translations.text: Or from meditation on whatever one wishes.

notes: Vyāsa: let him meditate on whatever he likes; a mind that has gained steadiness there gains it elsewhere too.

words.meaning: reaching from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude

translations.text: His mastery reaches from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude.

notes: Vyāsa: entering the subtle, the mind gains steadiness down to the smallest atom; entering the gross, up to the greatest magnitude. That it is unhindered as it runs to both limits is the highest mastery. Filled with it, the yogin's mind needs no further training by practice.

sanskrit.iast: kṣīṇavṛtter abhijātasyeva maṇer grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu tatsthatadañjanatā samāpattiḥ || 41 ||

lines.iast: kṣīṇavṛtter abhijātasyeva maṇer grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu tatsthatadañjanatā samāpattiḥ

padaccheda.iast: kṣīṇa-vṛtteḥ abhijātasya iva maṇeḥ grahītṛ-grahaṇa-grāhyeṣu tat-stha-tat-añjanatā samāpattiḥ
padaccheda.deva: क्षीण-वृत्तेः अभिजातस्य इव मणेः ग्रहीतृ-ग्रहण-ग्राह्येषु तत्-स्थ-तत्-अञ्जनता समापत्तिः

words.meaning: of (the mind) whose activities have dwindled
on the grasper, the grasping and the grasped
resting on that and taking its colour

translations.text: For the mind whose activities have dwindled, like a flawless gem, coalescence is its resting on the grasper, the grasping or the grasped and taking the colour of that.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘whose activities have dwindled’: whose cognitions have set. As a crystal, coloured by whatever it rests on, shines with the form of that, so the mind coloured by the object grasped shines with the form of that object: a subtle element, a gross thing, or the variety of the universe. So too with the organs, the means of grasping; and with the Puruṣa as grasper, and the freed Puruṣa. The grasper, grasping and grasped are the Puruṣa, the senses and the elements; the mind's standing in them and taking their form is called coalescence.

words.meaning: with the constructions of word, thing and knowledge

grammar.en: past passive participle f. nom. sg.

translations.text: Of these, coalescence with gross thought is that mixed with the constructions of word, thing and knowledge.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘cow’ the word, ‘cow’ the thing and ‘cow’ the knowledge are grasped as one though they are distinct; analysed, the properties of the word, of the thing and of the knowledge go separate ways. When the thing that has risen in the yogin's wisdom of absorption comes pierced by these constructions, the coalescence is mixed, and is called ‘with gross thought’.

translations.text: When memory is purified, (the coalescence) that is as if empty of its own form and shines as the object alone is without gross thought.

notes: Vyāsa: when memory is cleared of the conventions of words and of the constructions of knowledge from hearing and inference, the wisdom, coloured by the form of the object, as if gives up its own form as a grasping and becomes the object's form alone. That is the higher perception, the seed of scripture and inference. Its object is the whole (avayavin), such as a cow or a pot: a single thing, grasped by one cognition, that arises as a property common to the subtle elements. He argues against those who deny such a whole: without it nearly all knowledge would be false, and right knowledge would have no object.

sanskrit.deva: एतयैव सविचारा निर्विचारा च सूक्ष्मविषया व्याख्याता ॥ ४४ ॥
sanskrit.iast: etayaiva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣmaviṣayā vyākhyātā || 44 ||

lines.iast: etayaiva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣmaviṣayā vyākhyātā
lines.deva: एतयैव सविचारा निर्विचारा च सूक्ष्मविषया व्याख्याता

padaccheda.iast: etayā eva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣma-viṣayā vyākhyātā
padaccheda.deva: एतया एव सविचारा निर्विचारा च सूक्ष्म-विषया व्याख्याता

grammar.en: past passive participle f. nom. sg.

translations.text: By this same account are explained the coalescences with and without subtle thought, which have subtle objects.

notes: Vyāsa: coalescence in the subtle elements whose properties are manifest, limited by the experience of place, time and cause, is ‘with subtle thought’. That in them as unlimited by properties past, present or yet unnamed, and as the ground of all properties, is ‘without subtle thought’: the wisdom is then as if empty of its own form, the object alone. Those with and without gross thought have a gross object; these two a subtle one.

words.meaning: the having of a subtle object

translations.text: And the range of subtle objects ends in the unmarked.

notes: Vyāsa: for the atom of earth the subtle object is the subtle element of smell; for water, of taste; for fire, of colour; for air, of touch; for space, of sound. Subtler than these is the sense of ‘I’; subtler than that, the mere mark (liṅga-mātra, mahat); subtler than that, the unmarked (aliṅga, Prakṛti). Nothing is subtler than the unmarked. The Puruṣa is subtle too, but not in this line: he is not the material cause of the mark, only its occasion.

translations.text: These are meditative absorption with seed.

notes: Vyāsa: the four coalescences have an outer thing for their seed, so the absorption too is ‘with seed’: with and without gross thought on a gross object, with and without subtle thought on a subtle one.

words.meaning: in the clearness of (the absorption) without subtle thought

translations.text: In the clearness of the absorption without subtle thought there is the inner clarity.

notes: Vyāsa: clearness is the pure, steady flow of the sattva of the understanding, freed of the dirt that covers it and not overpowered by rajas and tamas. Then the yogin has the inner clarity: the light of wisdom, plain, whose object is the thing as it is, and which does not follow a sequence. As it is said: ‘Having climbed to the clarity of wisdom, the wise man, himself beyond grief, looks on all grieving people as one on a hill looks on those on the plain.’

translations.text: There wisdom is truth-bearing.

notes: Vyāsa: the wisdom born in the absorbed mind has this name, and it fits: it bears truth alone, with not a trace of error.

words.meaning: from the wisdom of scripture and of inference
because its object is the particular

translations.text: Its object is different from that of the wisdom of scripture and of inference, because its object is the particular.

notes: Vyāsa: scripture has the general for its object, since a word is not tied by convention to a particular; inference too ends in the general. A subtle, hidden or distant thing is not grasped by ordinary perception either. Yet the particular exists; it is grasped only by the wisdom of absorption, whether it belongs to a subtle element or to the Puruṣa.

translations.text: The latent impression born of that obstructs other impressions.

notes: Vyāsa: the impression born of the wisdom of absorption checks the store of impressions of the outward-turned mind; cognitions born of those then do not arise, and absorption sets in. From it comes wisdom, from wisdom new impressions, and so on. These do not give the mind a further task, for they cause the afflictions to waste away: the mind's striving ends in discernment.

padaccheda.iast: tasya api nirodhe sarva-nirodhāt nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ
padaccheda.deva: तस्य अपि निरोधे सर्व-निरोधात् निर्बीजः समाधिः

translations.text: On the cessation of that also, since all has ceased, there is seedless meditative absorption.

notes: Vyāsa: the impression born of cessation checks even the impressions born of absorption. The mind, with the impressions that lead to soleness, dissolves into its own source, Prakṛti, its task ended. When it has ceased, the Puruṣa rests in his own nature alone, and so is called pure, alone (kevala) and free.
